strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reducing inference cost of visual world-model planning with patch-token representations.
The proposed method is simple and lightweight: random token dropout during MPC rollouts and randomized grouped attention during training are easy to integrate into transformer-based world models.
The paper evaluates on six simulated visual control environments and compares against full-patch, CLS-token, and several token selection/merging baselines.
The analysis is reasonably thorough, including nHSIC, attentive probing, grouped-attention ablations, noise-robustness tests, and planning-time comparisons.
Empirically, moderate dropout often preserves or improves task success while reducing planning time, and random sampling is shown to be competitive with more sophisticated token selection methods.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: random token dropout is well known in ViT efficiency literature, and the main contribution is largely an application/inference-time adaptation of existing token-reduction ideas to world-model planning.

The practical impact is overstated: even at 50% dropout, planning can take tens of seconds per iteration (e.g., 82 s/iter in PushT), which is not close to real-time robotics, and all experiments are in simulation without real-world validation.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: success rates are reported without confidence intervals or error bars, several tasks use small evaluation sets, and some improvements over full-patch baselines may be within noise.

Baselines are somewhat narrow: the comparison focuses mainly on full-patch, CLS-token, and token-selection variants, but does not compare against other efficient world-model planning, model compression, or alternative planning architectures.

Several technical details are unclear, including exactly how randomized grouped attention is applied at inference under arbitrary token dropout, how the same token subset is enforced between predictions and the goal representation, and how attention masks interact with sparse inference.

Efficiency claims are not fully substantiated: speedups are sub-quadratic relative to dropout and are not decomposed into encoder, world-model, and planning costs; FLOPs, memory, and hardware-level latency are not reported.

Generality is limited: only DINO ViT-S/16 features are tested, the dropout rate requires per-environment tuning, and the very low Block Pushing success rates weaken conclusions on high-precision tasks.
Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and several implementation details and hyperparameter choices are only partially specified.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing inference cost of visual world-model planning under compute constraints.
The proposed random token dropout for MPC rollouts is simple and easy to integrate into transformer-based world models.
Uses randomized grouped attention during training as an interesting inductive bias intended to improve robustness to token subsets.
Broad empirical study across six simulated visual control environments.
Compares several token selection, pruning, and merging methods, and reports the useful negative result that sophisticated selection does not clearly outperform simple random dropout.
Provides planning-time measurements showing meaningful speedups at moderate dropout ratios in some settings.
Includes additional analyses such as nHSIC, attentive probing, grouped-attention ablation, and CEM noise robustness experiments.
The limitations section acknowledges simulation-only evaluation and encoder-specific scope.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: inference-time random token dropout is a simple, well-known idea in ViT efficiency, and applying it to world-model planning is incremental. The grouped-attention training trick is also relatively straightforward.

There is a core technical mismatch between training and inference: during training, tokens are not actually dropped; grouped attention only masks cross-group interactions while all tokens remain present. Thus the world model is not explicitly trained on arbitrary missing-token subsets, making the claimed generalization to sparse inference questionable.

The grouped-attention mechanism is underspecified: it is unclear how many groups are used beyond the stated two-group setup, how group sizes are sampled, how attention masks interact with causal temporal attention, how grouping is handled at inference after random dropout, and how positional information is preserved for dropped tokens.
Evaluation is limited to simulated environments using DINO features, despite the robotics and real-time motivation. No real-world or hardware-deployment evaluation is provided.

Efficiency claims are overstated. The paper claims real-time applicability, but reported planning times remain very large even with dropout, often tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration, and no FLOPs, memory, energy, or embedded-hardware latency analysis is given.

The central claim that task performance is preserved is not consistently supported. Some tasks degrade substantially at moderate-to-high dropout, and several apparent improvements over the full-token baseline are likely within noise given the small number of evaluation episodes.

No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for most success-rate comparisons, yet the paper makes strong comparative claims such as random dropout being comparable or better than sophisticated methods.

The comparison with token selection/merging baselines is not fully convincing. Results are mostly averaged across dropout ratios, some baselines are complex adaptations, and it is unclear whether they were tuned fairly under the same planning protocol.

The information-theoretic and probing analyses are narrow: they use only the Granular dataset, predict only coarse state summaries, and do not convincingly establish that the measured information is sufficient for planning performance across tasks.

The robustness analysis is weak: it assumes prediction errors behave like zero-mean Gaussian noise based on UMAP visual inspection and tests only Pointmaze with at most three MPC steps, which does not support broad robustness claims.
Missing comparisons to other efficient planning/world-model approaches beyond full-patch DINO-WM, CLS-token DINO-WM, and token pruning/merging methods weaken the positioning.

The conclusion that random dropout is sufficient may be task- and configuration-specific; the paper offers limited theoretical or mechanistic justification for why random sampling should be optimal beyond reference to ViT redundancy.
Clarity issues and overclaims remain: some wording is imprecise, methodological details are missing, and the paper presents stronger conclusions than the evidence supports for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: the high computational cost of patch-based visual world model planning, especially for MPC rollouts.
Proposes a simple and intuitive method, sparse imagination via random token dropout during inference, combined with randomized grouped attention training to handle arbitrary token subsets.
Provides a broad empirical study across six simulated visual control tasks, showing that moderate dropout preserves or sometimes improves success rates while reducing planning time.
Includes extensive analysis with nHSIC, attentive probing, grouped-attention ablations, and noise-robustness experiments to support the central claims.
Compares against multiple token selection and merging strategies, finding that simple random dropout is competitive or better, which is a useful practical insight.
Implementation details are mostly well documented in the appendix, and the limitations section honestly discusses simulation-only evaluation and hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: token dropout/reduction and DINO-based world model planning are existing ideas; the paper mainly combines them with a simple random inference-time dropout mechanism.
Evaluation is limited to simulated benchmarks and lacks real-robot validation, despite the motivation being real-time robotics under resource constraints.
Main success-rate results do not report variance or statistical significance, and some environments use relatively few evaluation episodes, making small differences hard to interpret.
Planning times remain high even with dropout (tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration in several tasks), so the claim of enabling real-time decision-making is not convincingly supported.
Baselines are limited mainly to Full-patch and CLS-token DINO-WM variants; comparisons to other efficient planning or token-reduced world-model methods are missing.

Some methodological details are underexplained, including whether the same token mask is shared between goal and observation features, exactly how CEM rollouts use dropout, and how grouped attention generalizes to arbitrary subsets at inference.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite otherwise detailed implementation descriptions.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reducing the computational cost of visual world model planning, especially for robotics and real-time deployment.
The proposed random token dropout is simple, near-zero overhead, and easy to integrate into existing transformer-based visual world models and VLA-guided planning pipelines.
Broad empirical coverage: multiple simulated control tasks, LIBERO-10, Meta-World, and real-world LeRobot tasks, with comparisons to full-patch, CLS-token, and several token-reduction baselines.
Provides useful analysis for why random sampling is surprisingly competitive, including the blind-spot problem, cluster-retention entropy, HSIC analysis, and attentive probing.
Ablations on grouped attention, different visual encoders, planning horizons, noise robustness, and adaptive dropout strengthen the empirical study.
The appendix is detailed, covering datasets, training, planning hyperparameters, and additional experiments, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: random token dropout/pruning is well studied in vision transformers, and applying random dropout during world-model planning is an incremental extension rather than a fundamentally new method.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: main success rates often have no confidence intervals or significance tests, several environments use only 20–60 evaluations, and real-world results are based on only 10 trials per task.
Some reported gains over the full-patch baseline may be within noise, as moderate dropout sometimes exceeds full-patch performance despite no clear mechanism for improvement.

The token-selection baselines are adapted in nontrivial ways for the planning setting, so their poor performance may partly reflect implementation choices rather than inherent limitations of importance-based selection.

Efficiency gains are moderate at practical dropout levels: at 50% dropout, average planning time reduction is around 40%, while more aggressive dropout often degrades performance; the real-world planner remains slower than the VLA-only baseline unless asynchronous inference is used.

The grouped-attention ablation may not fully isolate the benefit of the proposed training scheme versus merely training with sparse inputs, weakening the technical claim that randomized grouped attention is essential.

The paper argues for a general technique, but the scope is largely tied to DINO features and DINO-WM-style planning; comparisons to other efficient visual world-model or planning approaches are missing.

Some claims, such as 'significantly accelerates' and broad 'general technique' applicability, are stronger than the evidence provided, especially given the limited real-world evaluation and lack of released code or deployment details.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: the computational cost of visual world-model planning with many ViT patch tokens.
Proposes a simple inference-time random token dropout scheme and evaluates it across a broad set of simulated environments and real-world LeRobot tasks.
Includes extensive ablations and analyses, such as grouped attention, different visual encoders, adaptive dropout, noise robustness, and comparisons to token-selection baselines.
The empirical observation that sophisticated token-importance methods can fail due to a 'blind spot' problem is interesting and could motivate future work on dynamic token selection.
The appendix provides relatively detailed implementation and reproducibility information.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is random token dropout during planning, building directly on DINO-WM and prior token-reduction/dropout work; it feels more like an empirical recipe than a fundamentally new world-model or planning technique.

Technical soundness of the proposed randomized grouped attention is unclear: training with two random token groups and masked attention does not obviously train a model to process arbitrary sparse subsets at inference, and it is unclear how the group mask applies when arbitrary tokens are dropped at test time.

The central claim that random sampling is competitive or superior to importance-based selection is not sufficiently established: several token-selection baselines are adapted from classification/MAE settings, may not be fairly tuned for world-model planning, and some have different computational overheads.

Evaluation is statistically underpowered: many results use only 10-60 trials, lack confidence intervals or multiple seeds, and some tables average over drop ratios without a clearly specified protocol, making performance comparisons difficult to trust.

The 'blind spot' analysis, while interesting, is not conclusive as a fundamental explanation; it may reflect implementation or tuning issues in the baselines rather than an inherent failure of importance-based sampling.

The information-theoretic and probing analyses are only loosely connected to planning sufficiency; HSIC with state variables and probing of mean/std positions do not establish that sparse token subsets contain enough control-relevant information.

Efficiency claims are somewhat overstated: speedups at moderate drop ratios are real but often around 30-50%, and fixed encoder/environment costs limit gains; the reported numbers do not always support the language of dramatic acceleration.

Real-world evaluation is very limited: only two tasks, fixed goal images/proprioceptive states, small trial counts, and manually selected goals; this is far from a general real-time robotic deployment claim.

Clarity and consistency issues remain: the paper alternates between 'Drawer' and 'Printer' for real-world tasks, Table 4's handling of 'Fixed' for Granular/Rope is confusing, and the averaging protocol in Table 4 is unclear.
No code release is mentioned, and real-world data/checkpoints may be unavailable, limiting reproducibility of the strongest claims.

Positioning relative to prior efficient world models, token merging, and dynamic token selection for control is incomplete; the paper does not convincingly show why random dropout is the right abstraction rather than an incidental strong baseline.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: visual world-model planning is expensive, especially for real-time robotics, and proposes a simple inference-time token-dropping scheme to reduce cost.

The method is broadly applicable: random token dropout during latent rollout is compatible with different vision encoders, planning schemes (MPC-CEM, open-loop CEM, gradient-based planning), and VLA-guided action sampling.

Extensive empirical evaluation spans eight simulated environments plus real-world LeRobot tasks, with multiple baselines and ablations, demonstrating substantial planning-time reductions while often preserving task success.

Provides a useful and somewhat counterintuitive analysis of why random token sampling can outperform sophisticated importance-based token selection: static importance metrics create blind spots in dynamic planning, whereas random sampling maintains unbiased spatial coverage.
Supporting analyses such as HSIC, attentive probing, cluster-retention entropy, and blind-spot occurrence rates help explain the information redundancy and robustness behind the method.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: the appendix provides dataset details, hyperparameters, training settings, planning configurations, and additional ablations.
Generalization experiments across MoCo-v3, MAE, and DINOv3 encoders, as well as different planners and horizons, strengthen the claim that sparse imagination is a general efficiency technique.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: token dropout, grouped attention, and random token selection are existing ideas in ViT efficiency; the main contribution is their application to world-model planning, not a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: many results report only mean success rates without confidence intervals or significance tests, and some real-world/simulated evaluations use small numbers of trials (e.g., 10 real-world trials, 20-60 simulated evaluations), making it hard to judge whether small differences are meaningful.

The randomized grouped attention mechanism is not fully specified for inference. It is unclear how arbitrary token subsets are grouped or masked at planning time, which is central to the method and affects reproducibility.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around 'real-time' deployment: planner latencies remain on the order of seconds to tens of seconds per episode in key settings (e.g., LIBERO and real-world results), and the real-world evaluation uses manually selected goal images/states.

There are inconsistencies in real-world task naming/description (e.g., PickPlace, Drawer, Printer) and limited detail on how many real-world trials were completed per condition, which complicates interpretation.

The token-reduction comparison may under-tune baselines; differences between random sampling and several importance-based methods are often small and could fall within noise, while more computationally expensive selection methods may not be optimized for the same planning setup.

Performance is not uniformly preserved: some tasks/settings show clear degradation at moderate dropout (e.g., specific PointMaze/PushT ratios), and low absolute success on Block Pushing is hidden by aggregate averages.
The method assumes access to a suitable goal state/image and frozen pre-trained visual features; failure modes when the goal is ambiguous or encoder features are poor are only partially explored.
